title: Demystifying decisions makers' needs in sudden onset disasters
html:
Making decisions in a disaster can be very sensitive business. We always want to make the decision that will save the most lives, eliminate the most suffering or maximize aid efficiency. However, in a disaster, we often have to make rapid decisions with the limited information that we have on hand. This situation creates a type of “focusing illusion” where we take action based on what we see and know versus what we could know. And, as I outlined in a recent post about measuring impact, the decision may seem prudent at the time but can look irresponsibly negligent in hindsight. In decision making, looking back does not necessarily prepare us well for the future. We need to augment historical reviews by openly articulating what decisions we commonly need to make in emergencies, what information is needed for each decision, and what factors can influence these decisions.

A couple years ago, a small group of interested humanitarians from the Volunteer & Technical Communities, academia, UN-OCHA and ACAPS discussed the topic of humanitarian decision making and realized that we (as a larger community) needed to start mapping out the decisions made in emergencies and the related information requirements. We needed to help open up the humanitarian community in a way that external entities could help us. As we enter a Age of Context (mobile, social media, big data, senors and location), as defined by Robert Scoble and Shel Israel, we are going to need as much help as possible to make sure that we can distill the increasing amounts of data into the “little data” needed to respond effectively. In order to kick-start the process, UN-OCHA and ACAPS organized a workshop focused on Field-Based Decision Makers’ Information Needs in sudden onset disasters. Given the breadth of decision makers, we needed to focus our scope to ensure a concrete deliverable.

We held the workshop in late 2012 with the objective to create an initial framework for decision making and an initial scope of the information requirements in the first phases of a sudden onset disaster. We pulled in several very seasoned disaster responders and spent two days asking them questions and brainstorming with them. We focused on the early phases of an emergency and on decisions with scopes ranging from inter-agency to inter-cluster to cluster-specific to organization-specific. The workshop report, which we are releasing today, aims to allow others to prioritize their efforts toward important information and to organize their information in a manner intuitive and useful to humanitarian decision-makers. It provides a framework and set of information required by field-based decision-makers, a list of categories and types of decisions made by decision-makers, and a large set of brainstormed decisions from workshop participants.

Although the report is full of rich content, it is Table 12 (page 38) that comprehensively captures the “things” workshop participants wanted to know in a coherent and general framework. I found this table to perhaps be the most powerful piece of the report as it provides the general framework with a set of questions that we, as a community, could use to knowledgeably build out processes and solutions to support specific decisions/questions and eventually bring appropriate data into a large, overall emergency dashboard. Of course, others will find different pieces of the report more relevant. Table 8 outlines different Decision Dimensions: Time-frame, Scope, Locus/Authority, Criticality, Frequency/Duration, Information Gap, Function. Pivoting these dimensions onto each other creates different possible decision frameworks such as Figure 4 which combines Scope, Criticaclity and Information Gap. Essentially, we can now combine these different dimensions to better understand possible ways and influences on how people make decisions.

I believe that this report is a great start and will help us move forward in a structured way. Although information in each emergency may need to be framed slightly differently, we can start with the report’s framework and build out a predictable base to start with each time. Combining predictable information, in a structured and digestible format, with experienced responders will facilitate better, faster decisions thereby saving more lives, eliminating more suffering and improving aid efficiency.

Andrej

FYI: As a side note, I am happy to see organizations like Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF), who launched MSF Speaking Out, leading the way by opening up details around major decisions that they have made in the past so that others can more easily study and support the humanitarian community.
